chunks: How doping improves performance. The question: How does doping improve performance?
Doping improves silicon in four ways. It raises conductivity, since it adds many free carriers.
It makes the behavior steady, since the carrier count is fixed by the dopants and not by temperature.
It lets you choose electrons or holes, which is needed for diodes and transistors. And it lets you tune each region of a device for its own job.
Think of a river and a dam with adjustable gates. Pure silicon is like a trickle, whose flow changes a lot with weather.
Doping is like building controlled channels: more flow, a steady flow, and different channels for different jobs.
You can open one wide for low resistance and keep another narrow for high voltage. The analogy fails on one point: too much doping also makes things worse.
The undoped curve climbs about eight orders of magnitude over this range, which would make a resistor or junction unusable.
The doped curves are flat until the intrinsic density catches up: about 450-500 K for 10 to the 14 doping and about 600-700 K for 10 to the 16 .
That flat region is why doped devices are predictable. (Dopant freeze-out below roughly 100 K is not modelled.)
Conductivity: how easily a material carries current. It rises with the number of carriers.
Intrinsic carriers: free carriers in pure silicon, about 10 to the 10 per cm³ at room temperature. Doping level: dopant atoms per cm³, which sets the carrier count.
Junction: where N-type meets P-type. Breakdown voltage: the reverse voltage at which a junction starts to conduct heavily.
Pure silicon has about 10 to the 10 carriers per cm³. Dope it with 10 to the 16 phosphorus atoms per cm³. That is a million times more carriers.
The resistivity (the resistance of a 1 cm cube, in ohm-centimeters) falls from hundreds of thousands of ohm-centimeters to about half an ohm-centimeter.
The count now depends on the dopants, so it barely moves with temperature. That is the whole idea.
"Doping improves silicon in several ways.
It raises the carrier density by many orders of magnitude, so resistivity drops from hundreds of kilohm-centimetres to well under an ohm-centimetre.
It makes the carrier density set by design and stable over temperature instead of by thermal generation.
It lets me choose N or P so I can build junctions and transistors, and it lets me tune threshold, breakdown, gain and contact resistance.
The trade-off is that heavy doping lowers mobility and breakdown voltage."
